As the Buckley Court indicates, non-officers on the federal payroll are 
called “employees.” The Court’s definition—that “employees” are “lesser 
functionaries subordinate to officers”—does not do much to clarify the fine 
between these two categories. For example. Professor Mascott’s article, cited 
above, indicates that customs “weighers, gaugers, measurers and inspectors” 
would all have been considered “officers” in 1789, even if the duties of weighers, 
gaugers, and measurers, at least, were essentially nondiscretionary. Id. at 523. 
It is not clear how they would fare under the Buckley test. Mascott concedes as 
probably the most important counter-evidence to her view the fact that 
deputies to marshals and deputies to customs collectors were originally not 
treated as Officers of the United States for appointments purposes. She 
recognizes that such deputies “engaged in acts that significantly affected the 
rights of nongovernmental parties.” Id. at 515. But she says a “possible 
explanation” for the deputies’ non-officer status is that Congress understood 
them to be mere agents of the officials to whom they were deputies, noting, for 
example, that the appointing officials were Hable to private defendants for 
their deputies’ tortious acts. Id. at 516.
Freytag also had to confront an issue of what counts, constitutionally 
speaking, as a “department.” Although the Court was unanimous in concluding 
that special trial judges were inferior officers, the Court spHt five to four as to 
whether their appointment was permissible because the Chief Judge is the 
head of a “Department” within the meaning of Article II, or instead, because 
the Tax Court is a “court of law.” The majority took the latter approach, 
concluding that the appointments clause reference to “Courts of Law” was not 
limited to Article III courts, and that “a holding that every organ in the 
Executive Branch is a department would multiply indefinitely the actors 
ehgible to appoint.” Those concurring separately found it implausible to regard 
Article I tribunals as “Courts of Law” for constitutional purposes, and thought 
the reference to “Heads of Departments” logicaUy and historically must include 
“the heads of all agencies immediately below the President in the 
organizational structure of the Executive Branch.”
3. 
Assigning New Duties. Buckley tries to draw a categorical line around 
the means by which Congress can involve itself in the appointments process. 
One imaginable end-run for Congress might be to assign new duties to 
incumbent officers whose identities are already known. Shoemaker v. United 
States, 147 U.S. 282, 13 S. Ct. 361, 37 L.Ed. 170 (1893) dealt with creation of 
a five-member commission to supervise the development of Rock Creek Park 
in the District of Columbia. Congress provided that the President would 
appoint three of the members with the advice and consent of the Senate, but 
that the remaining two seats would go to the Army Chief of Engineers of the 
Army and to the Engineer Commissioner of the District of Columbia. Both were 
already commissioned as miHtary officers. The issue presented was whether 
they needed new appointments to undertake their additional responsibihties.
